newsitem.title: USA: Two rice breeders win World Food Prize.
newsitem.headline: Two rice breeders win World Food Prize.

text.p: Two plant scientists who developed rice varieties that allowed Asia to feed itself despite forecasts of famine were named on Tuesday as winners of the $200,000 World Food Prize.

Co-winner Henry Beachell developed a "miracle rice" that doubled yields as part of the Green Revolution of the 1960s. The other winner, Gurdev Singh Khush, was responsible for an early-maturing, high-yielding variety that is now the most widely planted rice on Earth.
The prize, given annually by a foundation, honors outstanding individual work to improve the world's food supply.

Beachell, 90, an American, and Khush, 61, born in India, did their seminal work at the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines. Khush, who began work at IRRI as an assistant to Beachell, has been its principal plant breeder since 1972.

Two years ago IRRI announced a new breed of thick-stalked "super rice" that could boost yields by 25 percent. It should be available to farmers in a few years, Khush said, after disease resistance is bred into it and its flavor is adapted for local tastes.
Rice is the most important food crop in developing countries. It is eaten by half the world's population.
Khush said it was "tremendously rewarding" to have aided farmers throughout Asia. "They are so proud of these breakthroughs," he said during an interview.

Despite the vast increases in output engendered by the new varieties, which confounded predictions of starvation in Asia, the future is even more daunting, Khush and Beachell said. Seventy percent more rice will be needed by 2025.
"It's a tremendous challenge to produce that much rice from the same (amount of) land with less (irrigation) water and fewer chemicals," Khush said.
Beachell went to work as a rice breeder for the U.S. Agriculture Department in Beaumont, Texas, on March 2, 1931. He eventually developed nine popular U.S. varieties before joining IRRI in 1963.

"As far as I'm concerned, the Green Revolution started right then (in 1931)," he said, describing how a primitive, back-breaking farming operation was transformed thanks to better varieties, fertilizers and mechanization.
The key to "miracle rice" from IRRI was to breed a shorter, faster-maturing plant that yielded more rice. Beachell spotted a "dwarf" variety while traveling in north Asia.
"It was simply an inherited trait. We moved that into a productive variety in a few years," he said.

IR8, as the thick-strawed, semi-dwarf rice was known, was developed in 1966. It was the highest yielding rice plant of its time and provided the genetic base for nearly all high-yielding rice grown in tropical and sub-tropical Asia.
Khush joined IRRI as a plant breeder in 1967 and worked with Beachell for years. His early-maturing, high-yield IR36 is planted on 2.7 million acres (11 million hectares).
IRRI varieties are planted on 70 percent of the world's rice land.
In 1987, Khush and Beachell were the first agricultural scientists to receive the Japan Prize, that nation's leading scientific prize.
